questions.stem: Which is an example of an ecosystem service provided by the natural environment?
options: Timber harvested from a plantation and sold to house builders
Wetlands filtering pollutants from water before it reaches rivers
Iron ore mined in the Pilbara and exported to steel mills overseas
A national park visited by bushwalkers on weekends and holidays
questions.explanation: Ecosystem services are the free work nature does, such as filtering water, pollinating crops and storing carbon. Ore and timber are natural resources, and a park enjoyed for recreation provides an amenity.

questions.stem: In the economy, the natural environment provides amenities. An amenity is:
options: a raw material such as coal or gas that is used as an input in production
a natural process, such as pollination, that supports farming and other industries
a sink that absorbs the waste and pollution created by production and consumption
a benefit people enjoy directly, such as a beach or scenic bushland for recreation
questions.explanation: Amenities are the direct enjoyment people get from the environment, such as recreation and beauty. Raw materials are natural resources, and pollination and waste absorption are ecosystem services.

questions.stem: Why do economists say that the natural environment is undervalued in market decisions?
options: Environmental goods are rivalrous, so firms compete them away before they can be sold
Consumers place no value at all on clean air or water when they make their spending choices
Many environmental services have no market price, so producers and consumers ignore them
Natural resources are always owned by the government, which sets their prices too high
questions.explanation: Services such as clean air, a stable climate and pollination are usually unpriced, so they do not enter private costs and benefits. People do value them, but markets fail to register that value.

questions.stem: Which is an example of the depletion of a non-renewable resource?
options: Clearing native vegetation for grazing faster than it can regrow
Extracting natural gas from a field until it is uneconomic to produce
Catching fish faster than the stock can breed and replace itself
Sending more household waste to landfill each year as household incomes rise
questions.explanation: Non-renewable resources such as gas, coal and oil form over geological time, so using them reduces the stock permanently. Fish and vegetation are renewable, but can be overexploited if harvested faster than they regenerate.

questions.stem: A fishery's catch rises for several years and then collapses as breeding stocks are exhausted. This illustrates:
options: overproduction of waste from consumption
the provision of an environmental amenity
overexploitation of a renewable resource
depletion of a non-renewable resource
questions.explanation: Fish stocks renew themselves only if harvests stay below the rate of natural replacement. Catching faster than that overexploits a renewable resource until it collapses.

questions.stem: Fishers in an open-access ocean fishery catch more than is sustainable. The main economic reason is that:
options: the government owns the fishery and sets catch limits far above what the stock can support
fish are a public good, so no fisher can be prevented from enjoying the fish without paying
the demand for fish is perfectly inelastic, so prices rise without limit as stocks fall
no one owns the stock, so each fisher gains from catching more while the cost of depletion is shared
questions.explanation: An open-access fishery is a common-pool resource: rivalrous but non-excludable. Without defined property rights each fisher ignores the cost of depletion to others, the tragedy of the commons. It is not a public good, because fish are rivalrous.

questions.stem: Climate change is mainly caused by:
options: changes in the sun's output that have increased solar radiation since the 1950s
rising volumes of household waste sent to landfill in developed countries
rising concentrations of greenhouse gases from burning fossil fuels and land clearing
the thinning of the ozone layer caused by chlorofluorocarbons in aerosols and fridges
questions.explanation: Burning coal, oil and gas and clearing forests add carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases to the atmosphere, trapping more heat. Ozone depletion is a separate problem.

questions.stem: Rising incomes lead households to buy more packaged goods and electronics, and landfill volumes grow. This environmental issue is best described as:
options: loss of an amenity
overproduction of waste
depletion of a non-renewable resource
overexploitation of a renewable resource
questions.explanation: Producers and consumers do not pay the full cost of disposal and pollution from waste, so too much is created. The issue concerns waste rather than the use of a resource stock.

questions.stem: A country's ecological footprint measures:
options: the biologically productive area needed to supply its consumption and absorb its waste
the total greenhouse gas emissions produced within its borders in a single year
the share of its land area that is protected in national parks and reserves
the dollar value of all the environmental damage caused by its industries over a full year
questions.explanation: The ecological footprint converts consumption and waste into the land and sea area, in global hectares, needed to sustain it. If a country's footprint exceeds its biocapacity it is using resources faster than they regenerate.

questions.stem: Greenhouse gas emissions are reported in tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2-e) because:
options: carbon dioxide is the only greenhouse gas that is produced by human activity
methane and nitrous oxide are measured in litres, which cannot be added to tonnes directly
the unit includes only emissions from electricity generation and transport
different gases trap different amounts of heat, so each is converted to a common unit
questions.explanation: Gases such as methane have a much stronger warming effect per tonne than carbon dioxide. Converting each to its CO2 equivalent lets total emissions be added and compared.

questions.stem: Country A has lower total emissions than Country B, but much higher emissions per person. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Country A must produce more output in total than Country B does each year
Country A contributes more to global warming in total than Country B does
Country A's emissions intensity per dollar of GDP must also be higher than Country B's intensity
Country A has a smaller population, but each resident is responsible for more emissions on average
questions.explanation: Lower total but higher per capita emissions means fewer people each emitting more. Total contribution to warming depends on total emissions, and emissions per dollar of GDP cannot be judged without output data.

questions.stem: Which greenhouse gas makes up the largest share of Australia's emissions, measured in CO2-e?
options: Water vapour
Carbon dioxide
Methane
Nitrous oxide
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels for electricity, transport and industry is by far the largest share. Methane, largely from livestock and fossil fuel extraction, is the next largest.

questions.stem: A country whose ecological footprint is larger than its biocapacity is:
options: producing less output per person than other countries of its size
protecting more land in national parks than it uses for farming
emitting fewer greenhouse gases than its forests can absorb each year
using resources faster than its own ecosystems can regenerate them
questions.explanation: Biocapacity is the ability of a country's ecosystems to supply resources and absorb waste. A footprint above it means an ecological deficit, met by drawing down natural capital or relying on other countries' resources.

questions.stem: Intergenerational equity means:
options: equal incomes for all age groups in the current population at a point in time
the transfer of wealth from parents to their children through inheritance
government payments that support today's retirees out of the taxes paid by younger workers
fairness between present and future generations in access to resources and environmental quality
questions.explanation: Intergenerational equity asks whether today's use of resources leaves future generations as well placed as we are. Inheritance is a private wealth transfer, not this principle.

questions.stem: How does environmental degradation threaten intergenerational equity?
options: Future generations will have higher incomes, so they can easily afford to restore the environment
Pollution today lowers current GDP, so present generations are worse off than future ones
Environmental damage is always reversed by market forces within one generation
Current output is raised by running down natural capital that future generations will need
questions.explanation: Depleting resources and damaging ecosystems shifts costs onto people not yet born, who cannot take part in today's decisions. There is no guarantee that damage can be undone later.

questions.stem: Sustainable development is often defined as development that meets present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs. Which policy best reflects this?
options: Approving new coal mines whenever they raise this year's real GDP growth
Subsidising petrol so that today's households pay less for transport
Allowing unlimited groundwater extraction during periods of drought
Setting fishing quotas below the rate at which the stock naturally replenishes
questions.explanation: Harvesting below the natural regeneration rate keeps the resource available for future generations. The other policies raise present consumption by running down resources or adding to emissions.

questions.stem: A negative externality in production occurs when:
options: a producer's own costs rise because the price of the raw materials it buys increases
consumers gain benefits from a product that the producer cannot charge for
the government taxes a producer for each unit of output that it sells
a producer's activity imposes costs on third parties that it does not pay for
questions.explanation: A negative externality is a spillover cost to people outside the transaction, such as pollution affecting nearby residents. Higher input prices are private costs the firm does pay.

questions.stem: A factory releases pollution into a river that harms downstream farmers. Because the factory ignores this cost, the market produces:
options: less than the socially optimal output, at a price that is too low
more than the socially optimal output, at a price that is too low
less than the socially optimal output, at a price that is too high
exactly the socially optimal output, as the farmers can sue later
questions.explanation: Marginal social cost exceeds marginal private cost, so the firm's supply curve lies below the true cost of production. The market equilibrium output is too high and the price too low.

questions.stem: On a demand and supply graph of a negative externality in production, the marginal social cost (MSC) curve lies:
options: above the demand curve, by the value of the benefit to third parties
along the same line as the demand curve, at the market equilibrium
above the marginal private cost (MPC) curve, by the external cost per unit
below the marginal private cost (MPC) curve, by the external cost per unit
questions.explanation: MSC = MPC + external cost, so MSC sits above the private supply curve. The socially optimal output is where MSC meets demand (marginal social benefit), at a lower quantity than the market produces.

questions.stem: On a negative externality graph, the market produces 800 tonnes where MPC equals demand, while MSC equals demand at 600 tonnes. The 200 tonnes between them represent:
options: overproduction, where the cost to society of each unit exceeds its benefit
underproduction, where the benefit to society of each unit exceeds its cost
the tax revenue the government collects when it corrects the externality
the amount of output that consumers would buy if the price were cut
questions.explanation: For each tonne between 600 and 800, marginal social cost is above marginal social benefit, so producing it makes society worse off. The resulting loss of welfare is the deadweight loss triangle.

questions.stem: Undefined property rights contribute to environmental overproduction because:
options: firms that pollute must pay compensation that raises their costs too far
consumers refuse to buy goods whose production has harmed the environment
no one can charge polluters for using the air or waterways they damage
governments own every natural resource and give it to firms free of charge
questions.explanation: When no one owns clean air or a river, the damage polluters cause has no price and is left out of their decisions. Clear property rights would let affected parties demand payment or bargain.

questions.stem: A household installs rooftop solar panels, reducing emissions from coal-fired electricity that would harm others. This is an example of:
options: a positive externality from consumption
a negative externality from production
a negative externality from consumption
a public good provided by government
questions.explanation: Third parties gain from lower emissions without paying for them, a spillover benefit from the household's purchase. The household decides only on its private benefit.

questions.stem: On a graph of a positive externality from consumption, the marginal social benefit (MSB) curve lies above the demand (MPB) curve. Without intervention, the market:
options: underproduces the good, with output below the socially optimal quantity
overproduces the good, with output above the socially optimal quantity
produces the socially optimal quantity, as supply equals marginal social benefit
underproduces the good, because the marginal social cost curve lies below supply
questions.explanation: Consumers buy where private benefit equals price, ignoring the benefit to others. The socially optimal output, where MSB meets supply, is larger, so the market underproduces environmental goods such as revegetation or clean energy.

questions.stem: Positive externalities lead to the underproduction of environmental goods such as tree planting because:
options: private buyers ignore the benefits to others, such as carbon storage and habitat
producers ignore costs imposed on third parties, such as pollution and noise
the government owns all land on which trees could be planted
the private benefits of planting trees always exceed the social benefits
questions.explanation: Those who plant trees capture only part of the benefit, while the community gains cleaner air, carbon storage and habitat for free. Demand based on private benefit is therefore too low.

questions.stem: Which is an economic cost of climate change to the Australian economy?
options: Higher numbers of tourists visiting healthier coral reefs
Lower farm output and incomes from more frequent and severe droughts
Lower global demand for renewable energy and critical minerals
Lower insurance premiums as the risk of property damage from storms falls
questions.explanation: Hotter, drier conditions and more extreme droughts reduce crop and livestock output. Climate change raises, rather than lowers, insurance costs, and coral bleaching harms reef tourism.

questions.stem: Rising sea levels and more intense storms are most likely to raise costs for Australian governments through:
options: repairing and protecting coastal infrastructure such as roads and sea walls
lower welfare spending as fewer people need disaster recovery payments each year
higher company tax revenue from firms in coastal tourist areas
falling demand for emergency services in regional communities
questions.explanation: Damage to coastal roads, ports and other infrastructure, plus disaster recovery payments, add to government spending. Disasters raise, not reduce, demand for welfare and emergency services.

questions.stem: Bushfires destroy homes and businesses, and rebuilding raises measured GDP for the following year. Why does this rise in GDP overstate the change in wellbeing?
options: GDP counts only exports, so domestic rebuilding activity is left out of the figures
Rebuilding replaces lost assets, while the destruction itself is never subtracted from GDP
The rebuilding is done mainly by overseas firms, so it is excluded from GDP entirely
Spending on reconstruction is counted as a transfer payment rather than output
questions.explanation: GDP counts the new output of rebuilding but makes no deduction for the homes, forests and businesses lost. The community is not better off for having replaced what it already had.

questions.stem: Increased heatwaves are likely to reduce labour productivity in Australia mainly because:
options: outdoor work in industries such as construction and farming becomes slower or unsafe
workers move to higher-paid jobs in air-conditioned offices in cooler countries overseas
businesses replace workers with machines that run on renewable energy
the government lowers the minimum wage in very hot regions
questions.explanation: Extreme heat makes physical work less safe and less productive, cutting hours and output in exposed industries. It also adds health costs.

questions.stem: Which sector has been the largest single source of Australia's greenhouse gas emissions?
options: Domestic aviation and shipping
Electricity generation
Waste management
Industrial processes
questions.explanation: Australia's heavy reliance on coal-fired power made electricity the largest source of emissions. Transport, stationary energy and agriculture are also major sources, while waste is comparatively small.

questions.stem: Australia's national emissions have fallen below 2005 levels. Which factor has been the largest contributor to this fall over the period?
options: Lower emissions from land use and land clearing
A large fall in emissions from road transport
The closure of most of the country's gas fields
A sharp fall in the size of the national population since 2005
questions.explanation: Much of the fall since 2005 came from reduced land clearing, recorded under land use, land-use change and forestry. Renewable electricity has added to the fall, while transport emissions have tended to rise with population and vehicle use.

questions.stem: Which development has helped reduce emissions from Australia's electricity sector?
options: A rise in the share of electricity produced from diesel
A fall in the use of batteries and pumped hydro for storage
Growth in wind and solar generation, including rooftop solar
Growth in the number of new coal-fired power stations built
questions.explanation: Wind farms, solar farms and rooftop solar have taken a growing share of generation, lowering emissions per unit of electricity. Diesel and new coal plants would raise emissions.

questions.stem: Compared with most other developed countries, Australia's greenhouse gas emissions per person are:
options: relatively high
relatively low
about average
among the world's lowest
questions.explanation: Reliance on coal for electricity, large distances and energy-intensive mining and agriculture give Australia high emissions per person by developed-country standards.

questions.stem: A scatterplot of countries shows GDP per capita on the horizontal axis and emissions per capita on the vertical axis. The points slope upwards, with a few wealthy countries well below the trend. The best interpretation is:
options: richer countries tend to emit more per person, but high income without high emissions is possible
higher emissions cause countries to become richer, as the upward slope proves
income and emissions are unrelated, since some countries lie below the trend line
poorer countries emit more per person than richer countries do on average
questions.explanation: The upward slope shows a positive relationship between income and emissions per person. The outliers show that energy sources and policy matter, and correlation alone does not show which causes which.

questions.stem: A table shows a country's emissions fell by 10% over a decade while real GDP rose by 25%. This shows that:
options: real GDP growth must have been caused by the fall in emissions
the country's ecological footprint must have fallen by 25%
emissions intensity of output fell, so growth was decoupled from emissions
emissions intensity of output rose, as output grew faster than emissions
questions.explanation: Output rose while emissions fell, so emissions per dollar of GDP fell sharply: absolute decoupling. The data do not show cause and effect or measure the ecological footprint.

questions.stem: A time-series line graph shows Australia's emissions from transport rising steadily over two decades. Which factor best explains this trend?
options: Growth in population, vehicle numbers and freight moved by road
A switch from petrol cars to electric vehicles across the fleet
A fall in the distance travelled by households and businesses
The closure of coal-fired power stations in several states
questions.explanation: More people, cars and road freight mean more fuel burnt. A shift to electric vehicles would lower transport emissions, and power station closures affect the electricity sector.

questions.stem: A column chart shows that a mining region produces a large share of a state's output and a large share of its emissions. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Reducing the region's emissions will have no effect on the state's output
Mining in the region produces no externalities for third parties elsewhere
Production in the region is emissions-intensive, linking the environment and output
The region's emissions are caused by household consumption rather than production
questions.explanation: The chart links the region's production to its emissions, showing the relationship between the natural environment and output. Cutting emissions there may involve costs to output unless cleaner methods are adopted.
